Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need help getting a clear prompt together for the inventory note at harbor street food cooperative. the count happened on april 18, after the thursday receiving shift and before the doors opened for the afternoon pickup. ask for a practical inventory reconciliation memo for the board packet, not a sales announcement or a general description of the co-op. it should help people see what was counted, where the figures disagree, and what still needs checking. use only the notes and numbers i give here. do not open cloud links. you may read the pasted text and the files attached directly to this conversation; the paper binder is also available at the front desk if you need to check a name or unit label. no one has asked for a purchase recommendation, and i don't have prices in these notes, so don't make up costs or a budget.

There is a pencilled note beside the oats that says “one torn sack, still on the shelf.” don't turn that note into a quantity loss; it doesn't give a weight or say that any oats were discarded.

in the cooler, Jo's page lists 14 cartons of oat milk, 8 cartons of whole milk, 11 blocks of tofu, and 6 crates of apples. a second handwritten line, below the main list, says “2 oat milk held for Friday pickup.” the page doesn't say whether those two cartons are already included in the 14 or set aside separately, and the pickup list isn't included here. keep that uncertainty visible instead of choosing one interpretation. the cooler sheet also has a temperature reading of 4°C at 10:20 a.m. and 5°C at 12:05 p.m. do not describe either reading as proof of a problem or as proof that the cooler was fine; the note only records the readings. Jo wrote that the door was opened several times during receiving, but didn't record how long it stayed open.

at the pickup door, Amira counted 7 crates of apples and 3 boxes of tomatoes. the apple crates have the same green labels as the crates in the cooler, but there is no transfer slip or other note showing whether these are separate crates. one customer order sheet says 2 crates of apples were due for collection at noon; it is not marked collected or uncollected. Include both details, and don't combine the apple counts across locations or subtract the order. Amira also wrote “tomatoes moved in from the garden table?” with a question mark. there is no garden-table count in the information i have, so leave that as an unresolved note rather than saying the tomatoes came from there.

please structure the memo so a board member can scan it without losing the distinctions in the source notes. use a short opening that identifies the date and scope, then a section for each of the three locations, followed by a brief section for items or records that need checking. a compact table is fine if the labels make clear which numbers are observed counts, receiving-log details, or pickup notes. keep the units exactly as written: bags, cans, jars, tins, cartons, blocks, crates, and boxes. don't convert cases into a new counted stock total. at the end, list the specific follow-up questions raised by these records: whether the rice delivery was shelved before counting; whether the chickpea delivery and shelf count can be reconciled; whether the two oat-milk cartons are included in the 14; whether the apples at the two locations are separate stock; whether the noon apple order was collected; and what the tomato question-mark note refers to. include the cooler readings and the torn-sack note among items to review, but don't turn either one into a finding. The count took place on April 18, after the Thursday receiving shift and before the doors opened for the afternoon pickup. Explain what was counted, where the figures disagree, and what still needs checking. Do not write a sales announcement or a general description of the co-op. Use only the information below. Do not open cloud links. You may read the pasted text and files attached directly to this conversation; the paper binder is also available at the front desk if you need to check a name or unit label. Keep the three count locations separate: the main dry-goods room, the walk-in cooler, and the small table by the pickup door. Items may be moved between locations during a shift, but the records do not establish that any move happened on April 18. Len and Priya counted the dry-goods room. Jo counted the cooler, with Len reading the sheet aloud. Amira counted the pickup table alone. These names identify the counters; they are not approvals or sign-offs. The count sheet was completed on paper, and the shift lead typed the figures below from it on April 19. Note that date difference so the typed copy is not mistaken for a second count.

### 1. Main dry-goods room

The April 18 count sheet lists 24 bags of brown rice, 18 bags of rolled oats, 31 cans of chickpeas, 12 jars of tomato passata, and 9 tins of coconut milk. The receiving log records 6 bags of brown rice delivered on April 17, but does not say whether they were put into the dry-goods room before the count. It also records 4 cases of chickpeas on April 17, with 12 cans per case, signed by Len. The count sheet gives no separate case count, only cans. Show the stated count and the relevant receiving entry next to each other without silently adding or subtracting the delivery. A pencilled note beside the oats says, “one torn sack, still on the shelf.” Do not treat this as a quantity loss: it gives no weight and does not say that any oats were discarded.

### 2. Walk-in cooler

Jo’s page lists 14 cartons of oat milk, 8 cartons of whole milk, 11 blocks of tofu, and 6 crates of apples. A second handwritten line below the main list says, “2 oat milk held for Friday pickup.” The page does not say whether these two cartons are included in the 14 or set aside separately, and the pickup list is not provided. Keep that uncertainty visible rather than choosing an interpretation.

The cooler sheet records a temperature of 4°C at 10:20 a.m. and 5°C at 12:05 p.m. Do not describe either reading as proof of a problem or as proof that the cooler was fine; the note only records the readings. Jo also wrote that the door was opened several times during receiving, without recording how long it stayed open.

### 3. Pickup table by the door

Amira counted 7 crates of apples and 3 boxes of tomatoes. The apple crates have the same green labels as the crates in the cooler, but there is no transfer slip or other note showing whether these are separate crates. A customer order sheet says 2 crates of apples were due for collection at noon; it is not marked collected or uncollected. Include both details, but do not combine the apple counts across locations or subtract the order. Amira also wrote, “tomatoes moved in from the garden table?” There is no garden-table count in the available information, so leave this as an unresolved note rather than saying the tomatoes came from there.

### 4. Presentation and checks

Use a short opening that identifies the date and scope, then a section for each location, followed by a brief section for items or records that need checking. A compact table is acceptable if its labels distinguish observed counts from receiving-log details and pickup notes. Keep the units exactly as written: bags, cans, jars, tins, cartons, blocks, crates, and boxes. Do not convert cases into a new counted stock total. If a calculation is useful, show which source figures it uses and label it as arithmetic from the receiving log, not a verified recount. Do not present a calculated total as a confirmed physical count.

List these follow-up questions at the end: Was the rice delivery shelved before counting? Can the chickpea delivery and shelf count be reconciled? Are the two oat-milk cartons included in the 14? Are the apples at the two locations separate stock? Was the noon apple order collected? What does the tomato question-mark note refer to? Include the cooler readings and torn-sack note among items to review, but do not turn either into a finding.

Marta, who was sorting the papers, said, “I can check the original sheets after the weekend, but I don't know who moved the apple crates.” Keep this as a quoted report from Marta, not as confirmation that crates were moved. Keep the memo neutral and useful for the board packet, and finish with the unresolved checks rather than an assumed explanation or recommendation."}]
